question_text: Find the general solution of dy/dx = e^(x+y).

insider_note: e^(x+y) splits as e^x·e^y purely because of the exponent law e^(a+b) = e^a·e^b — that split is what turns an otherwise mixed equation into one where x and y separate cleanly.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Use e^(x+y) = e^x·e^y first, then move every y term to one side and every x term to the other.
steps.memory_tip: e^(x+y) = e^x·e^y is the exponent law that unlocks separation here — always split a sum in the exponent this way first.
lines: Given D.E is dy/dx = e^(x+y) = e^x·e^y
⇒ dy/e^y = e^x·dx ⇒ e^(−y)dy = e^x dx ⇒ e^x dx − e^(−y) dy = 0
steps.why: Splitting e^(x+y) into e^x·e^y using the exponent addition law separates the equation at once, since every y term can then be moved to one side and every x term to the other with no x and y ever mixed together.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate e^(x+y) directly as a single exponential without splitting it first.
Dividing by e^y but forgetting to flip its sign to e^(−y) when moving it across.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. ∫e^x dx = e^x and ∫e^(−y) dy = −e^(−y); combine them with a single constant c.
steps.memory_tip: ∫e^(−y)dy = −e^(−y), with a minus sign from the chain rule on the negative exponent — easy to drop by mistake.
steps.why: Integrating each side separately gives e^x on one side and −(−e^(−y)) = e^(−y) on the other once the minus signs are tracked correctly, and combining both with a single arbitrary constant gives the final relation.
common_mistakes: Losing track of the minus sign and writing the final answer as e^x − e^(−y) = c.
Integrating e^(−y) as e^(−y) instead of −e^(−y), and so getting the sign of the second term wrong.
